newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia set for ASEAN team, king signals dissent.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia set for ASEAN team, king signals dissent.

text.p: Cambodia on Tuesday welcomed efforts by the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to help restore political stability in the strife-torn country and invited a delegation to visit within days.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi said he had received a letter from Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot, on behalf of strongman Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, welcoming an ASEAN mediation mission to Phnom Penh.

At the same time, political analysts labelled King Norodom Sihanouk's refusal on Monday to endorse a new co-premier to replace his ousted son as a sign of the monarch's disapproval of Hun Sen's takeover of power in a bloody putsch in the capital on July 5 and 6.
Ung Huot stated in his letter, which he said was sent on behalf of Hun Sen: "I have the pleasure to reconfirm that Cambodia welcomes ASEAN's role to help restore political stability to the country...
"I would like to invite you, Excellencies... to come to Cambodia at a date convenient to them, if possible this week."

Hun Sen rebuffed an earlier mediation mission, led by Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas and including the Thai and Philippine foreign ministers, after he ousted his coalition partner, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, in fighting between their forces.
Ranariddh was in Paris at the time and since then has visited the United States and some Asian capitals to win support for his position.
Last Friday Hun Sen said ASEAN's role in ensuring political stability in Cambodia should be limited to preventing outside interference.
An aide to Hun Sen said the second prime minister's position on intervention had not changed and he would discuss ASEAN's role with the delegation.
"Hun Sen's position has remained the same all along," Prak Sokhonn told Reuters.

"He welcomes constructive discussion with ASEAN representatives and we expect the delegation to come to Phnom Penh again this week," he said. "Their role has to be discussed between the delegates and Hun Sen."
A Phnom Penh-based diplomat said the fact that Tuesday's message to ASEAN did not reiterate that the group's role should be limited to preventing interference was an encouraging sign.
"I think the omission of that phrase is significant," the diplomat said. "Hun Sen is making another little gesture."
Ung Huot said on Tuesday that King Sihanouk's refusal to recognise his nomination as first prime minister was premature since the nation's parliament had yet to decide on the issue.
Sihanouk said from Beijing on Monday that he would not recognise Ung Huot as first prime minister as the position belonged to his son, Ranariddh.
Ung Huot, a senior member of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, was nominated to replace Ranariddh by party members who remained in Cambodia after the prince's overthrow by Hun Sen on July 6.

Hun Sen backs Ung Huot's nomination to replace Ranariddh, but the prince, in his capacity as president of FUNCINPEC, expelled Ung Huot from the party last weekend. Ung Huot dismissed the move as an act of desperation and a joke.
Diplomats said the king, by withholding his endorsement, was probably not trying to prevent Ung Huot's appointment by the National Assembly. That is expected in the next few days.
"I don't think it will derail the process," said a diplomat. "The king has clearly said in an earlier statement that the acting head of state can approve motions.
"I think it's more of an indication of his disapproval of what's been going on and a sign he clearly wants to stay in the game.
"He obviously doesn't approve of what Hun Sen has done and if he were to fully endorse Ung Huot's appointment it would be difficult to retreat from that position," the diplomat said.
The king is required by the constitution to "designate" a new prime minister but political analysts said such technicalities were unlikely to block Hun Sen's plans.
"I don't think it's going to even be raised," said another diplomat.
"Hun Sen is not going to let these sort of details get in his way," said a political analyst.

Cambodia had been due to join ASEAN last week along with Burma and Laos, but its membership was put on hold because of the political crisis there. ASEAN currently comprises Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
A Cambodian government official said on Tuesday that the fighting in Phnom Penh in early July and subsequent looting by victorious Hun Sen forces caused more than $70 million of damage.

Cambodians on Tuesday also got their first glimpse in years of hated Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot -- looking old and frail -- when the U.S. ABC-TV News showed an exclusive video of his "trial" last week in the northern guerrilla stronghold of Anlong Veng.

Pol Pot's regime was held responsible for the death of more than one million Cambodians, and he has not been seen by outsiders since 1979, after he was ousted from Phnom Penh by a Vietnamese-backed invasion.
